<!-- P01 -->
Everything here is free or free to try, already exists, and was built for people in your
position. None of it requires a purchase order.

The sections answer different questions. Where do I get material I don't have time to
write? Where do students actually put their hands on something? What do I point the
interested ones at? And when an administrator asks what standard this maps to, what do I
say?

<!-- P02 -->
## Curriculum you can take and use

Writing a unit from nothing is the slowest way to teach cybersecurity.

[Teach Cyber](https://www.teachcyber.org/) is built specifically for secondary
cybersecurity teachers, and it carries professional development alongside the curriculum.
If you are teaching this for the first time, start here.

[Cyber.org](https://cyber.org/) covers the full K-12 range and has a "Find Curricula" tool
that filters to your grade band.

[CLARK Center](https://clark.center/) is a reviewed digital library of cybersecurity
curriculum, searchable by topic, grade band, and how much class time you actually have.
Lessons arrive with objectives and materials attached, so you can search for something that
fits your week instead of building it. CLARK4Kids is the younger-learner arm, with units
like Online Gaming Safety and Password Pros.

[NCYTE](https://www.ncyte.net/), the National Cybersecurity Training and Education Center,
is faculty-facing and skews toward the postsecondary end.

[RING](https://www.ring-cyber.org/) is a free online cybersecurity course for students and
educators.

[CodeHS](https://codehs.com/curriculum/cybersecurity) runs a structured 6-12 cybersecurity
sequence on its own platform, which suits a school already using CodeHS for CS.

[Supplement to CSEC 2017](https://doi.org/10.1145/3715982), *Foundational Cybersecurity
Content and Instructional Guidance for Secondary and Postsecondary Cybersecurity Education*
(ACM, January 2025). The original CSEC 2017 guidelines were written for university degree
programs. This supplement extends them to secondary education, which makes it the closest
thing that exists to an authoritative answer to "what should a high school cybersecurity
course cover?" You teach from CLARK. You cite this when someone asks you to justify what
you chose to teach.

<!-- P03 -->
## Hands-on environments

Reading about a network and breaking one are different activities, and the second is what
students remember.

[CyberHub](https://saguaroscyberhub.org) is the Cyber Saguaros' platform at the University
of Arizona, described on the site as "the official cybersecurity lab, cyber warfare range,
and eLearning platform." Four things live there. The Crucible is a capture-the-flag
environment with isolated practice lanes and live scoring. CyberLabs provides on-demand
virtual environments for coursework and practice. The Forge is a malware analysis sandbox.
And Clinic-in-a-Box is what the Day 2 afternoon tabletop runs on, an AI-assisted tool that
walks a team through a cyber risk assessment against a mock client. If you want to run that
exercise again with your own students, that is where it lives. Access requires an account,
and whether that extends to educators outside the University of Arizona is a question for
Paul Wagner.

[US Cyber Range](https://www.uscyberrange.org/) offers secure cloud-based environments for
student practice.

Cyber Arena comes through the National Cybersecurity Teaching Academy. It was supplied
without a link, so ask Paul Wagner for the access route.

CSforAR, Domain 5 runs professional development on networking and cybersecurity, including
building networks with Raspberry Pi computers. Arkansas-specific, and the one item on this
page most likely to already have a person attached to it in your district.

<!-- P04 -->
## Competitions

Competitions do something a lesson can't: they give a student a reason to keep going after
the bell. All three run on their own calendars, so check when registration opens before you
look at anything else.

[CyberPatriot](https://www.uscyberpatriot.org/) is the Air & Space Forces Association's
national youth cyber program and the most K-12-native option here. Teams compete to defend
virtual networks, and the program is built for a teacher-coach who isn't a security
professional.

[National Cyber League](https://nationalcyberleague.org/) runs individual and team
capture-the-flag competitions, pitched older than CyberPatriot.

[SANS Holiday Hack Challenge](https://www.sans.org/cyber-ranges/holiday-hack-challenge) is
free, annual, and deliberately approachable. A student can try it alone over a break
without you organizing anything, which makes it a cheap way to find out which of your
students light up when handed a real puzzle.

<!-- P05 -->
## AI in the classroom

[MagicSchool](https://www.magicschool.ai/) is the teacher-facing tool used in these PD
sessions for classifying data, exploring data pictures, and building out solutions.

[Machine Learning for Kids](https://machinelearningforkids.co.uk/) lets students build and
break small models in a browser, on data they choose themselves. Good for showing the
limits of a model rather than describing them.

[NC State AI Teaching Resources](https://teaching-resources.delta.ncsu.edu/ai-prompting-basics/)
covers prompting basics for instructors.

[Turnitin: guiding responsible AI prompts](https://www.turnitin.com/blog/6-ways-to-guide-responsible-ai-prompts-for-learning).

[Databricks: AI literacy](https://www.databricks.com/blog/ai-literacy).

Both of those last two are vendor-authored. Useful, and read them knowing who wrote them.

<!-- P06 -->
## Careers and work roles

[IBM SkillsBuild](https://skillsbuild.org/) has a student-facing catalog for exploring
cybersecurity career paths.

[NICE Framework](https://niccs.cisa.gov/tools/nice-framework) is the NIST National
Initiative for Cybersecurity Education framework, published through CISA. It describes
cybersecurity work as roles, tasks, knowledge, and skills, and it is the vocabulary most
American funding and pathway documents are written in.

[DoD Cyber Workforce Framework](https://dodcio.defense.gov/Cyber-Workforce/DCWF/) is the
Department of Defense's own version. It matters if your students may head toward federal or
defense-contractor work, and it does not line up cleanly with NICE.

One caution, because it will save you an argument later. These frameworks describe
*professional* work at a level of detail K-12 standards do not, so a lesson does not cleanly
"map to" a NICE work role no matter how much a form wants it to. Claim alignment where you
can defend it and say so plainly where you can't. A partial map you can defend will hold up.
A complete one won't survive the first person who checks it.

<!-- P07 -->
## The CAE community

If your school is anywhere near a cybersecurity pathway conversation, this is where the
national infrastructure lives.

[CAE Community](https://www.caecommunity.org/) is the hub for the National Centers of
Academic Excellence in Cybersecurity: professional development, working groups, and the
people to ask. Membership costs nothing and it is the fastest route to a colleague who has
already solved your problem.

[CAE Resource Directory](https://caeresource.directory/browse) indexes what that community
has produced, including labs, modules, outreach materials, and competition prep. It is
broader and less curated than CLARK, so go there when you know roughly what you want but
not what it is called.

[NCAE-C Document Library](https://www.cyber.mil/ncae-c/document-library) holds the official
designation documents and Knowledge Units. It is the primary source, which matters when a
claim has to survive scrutiny.
